note: No holdout. Owner directed 2026-09-03 to use the full period. Every balance below is in-sample.
phase: 12-signal battery on two asset classes; cross-asset replication culls 6 survivors to 1 robust factor

worse everywhere; best $1298.
NEW LEADER. breakout + ma gate + trendMa 200: $3424.62 on 156 trades at 12.43% maxDD.
200 is an interior peak, but a sharp one: 150 $3373, 200 $3425, 250 $2282, 300 $1590.

sweptAxes.axis: maxHold x minStopPct x maxStopPct, gated
sweptAxes.result: small gain. minStopPct 0.03 beats 0.05: $3543.12 on 160 trades at 13.99% DD. With the gate on, maxHold 100 now beats 200/400/800 -- the opposite of the ungated sweep4.

five new filters, none of them material. Best is atrPctBand min 3% at $3672.04 (+3.6%) by dropping 5 of 160 trades; btcRegime 100 is $3656.32 by dropping 17. Removing a handful of losers from a 156-trade sample moves the balance a few percent by chance, so treat these as unswept rather than as working filters.

clearly worse. Best is bos/trendMa600/minStop3%/hold300 at $1630 with a 73.72% drawdown, against the daily leader's $3672 at 13.99%. Six times the bars means six times the trades and six times the cost; the campaign's cost identity (0.017/stopPct per trade) does not care that the bars are shorter. The daily timeframe is where this works.

banking any of a runner hurts, monotonically. Best is the smallest possible bank (25% at 12R) at $3010.25 against $3543.12 with no partial; taking 75% off at 5R gives $2107. This is the concentration finding restated as a control: the tail IS the return, so realising part of it removes the return.

INVALID for breakout and bos. stopMode is only implemented for entryMode anticipate, so seven atrStopK values produced seven byte-identical rows. Those 14 rows are marked invalid in the log and backtestMultiTF now throws instead of ignoring the parameter. anticipate does respond: atrStopK 3 gives $1928.99 at a 10.51% drawdown on 98 trades, still below the structural leader.

atrPctBand + btcRegime is the best pair at $3760.75 (13.51% DD). Adding adx or maSlope always LOWERS the balance and always LOWERS the drawdown -- all four together give $2624.88 at 8.57% DD on 78 trades. A real risk/return trade, no free lunch.

sweptAxes.axis: breakeven lock on the gated leader
sweptAxes.result: arming the lock LATER helps: beTriggerR 3 with beLockR 0.2 gives $3885.34 against $3543.12 at the 2.0 default. Consistent with the tail thesis -- an early breakeven stop chokes the runners that carry the return.

sweptAxes.axis: swing window x breakout lookback x alignMode
sweptAxes.result: n and alignMode are BOTH no-ops for breakout. alignMode is structurally dead in a single-timeframe run (no higher TFs exist, so every mode evaluates true) -- do not sweep it again without a multi-TF series. breakoutLookback does bind; 20 is best.

sweptAxes.axis: beTriggerR x filters x trendMa combined
sweptAxes.result: NEW LEADER. $4077.96 on 148 trades at 13.54% DD -- level with buy-and-hold BTC ($4105.94) at roughly a quarter of its 52.06% drawdown.

Built the last idea from the literature search: rank the universe by trailing Sharpe and trade only the leaders. It does NOT help returns. Tighter selection monotonically lowers the balance and lowers the drawdown, the same risk/return dial every other filter turned out to be: topN 12 gives $3685.85 at 10.96% DD, topN 3 gives $2363.77 at 7.81%. The nominal new best, topN 20 of 29 pairs at $4175.64, filters almost nothing -- it drops 5 trades of 148 for +2.4%, which is noise at this sample size, not selection working.

sweptAxes.axis: higherTfs x alignMode x swing window
sweptAxes.result: Adding a higher timeframe to the breakout leader collapses it: 143 trades to 71, $4175.64 to $1289.87. The cause is not alignment -- alignMode and n were flagged INERT by the new detector, byte-identical across every value. It is that trendSrc is the HIGHEST timeframe present, so a 3-day series turns the 200-period MA gate into a 600-day lookback. Supplying a higher timeframe is not an alignment-only change.

sweptAxes.axis: alignMode where it is actually wired
sweptAxes.result: bos and anticipate are the only modes that consult alignMode, and only with a higher timeframe present. Swept there it genuinely binds -- anticipate on a weekly anchor gives 237 trades/$2390 at alignMode none against 162/$2539 at first -- but nothing beats the leader. Best is $3833.05 (anticipate, 3-day anchor, alignMode none, trendMa 20) at a 21.77% drawdown. 'first' and 'all' are identical with a single higher timeframe, as they must be.

Raw sweep runs to $16,138 at volTarget 0.10 / clamp 5, and that number is LEVERAGE -- the universe's median trade sits at 5.55% ATR, so a 10% target scales every bet up and deploys 3.7x the risk. Risk-matched (equity.mjs riskMatchedRiskPct holds mean deployed risk at 0.5%) the real answer is $5087 against $4175.64 flat, at 13.41% drawdown against 13.54% -- and it is FLAT across volTarget 0.03-0.10 at any clamp >= 3. That plateau is the point: once the clamp is loose the weights are just proportional to 1/ATR% and the level cancels, so there is one structural decision here and no threshold to fit. First such change in the campaign.

Filling on the NEXT bar's open instead of the signal bar's close IMPROVES the result: $4874.70 against $4595.23, and it wins on every robustness margin -- worst-pair-out $3723 vs $3480, full-history $3636 vs $3431, drop-ten-best $1125 vs $1049, and higher mean R in all three years. Mechanically it declines to buy the close of the breakout day, which is the top of that day's move. Two bars collapses to $2305, so this is a discontinuity rather than a curve. Adopted, because it is both the more realistic assumption and the better one. feeBufferPct barely matters below 0.05.

The strongest evidence so far that the result is not a cost-model artifact. At 3x the modelled fee (2.4% vs 0.8%) AND 40x the modelled slippage (2% vs 0.05%) the strategy still ends at $2580.11, above the $1419.93 equal-weight basket. At 2x fees and 10x slippage it is $3458.78. It degrades smoothly and stays positive across the whole grid.

Capping simultaneous positions at 3 and raising per-position risk to 1% gives $5160.44 at an 8.96% drawdown, against the unlimited book's $4874.70 at 12.94%. More return, less drawdown, and LESS capital at risk at the peak: 3 x 1% = 3% against 19 x 0.5% = 9.5%. The nineteen concurrent longs were largely the same bet nineteen times.

Every one of 27 configurations loses. Best $993.06 at a 49.48% drawdown. Run without a trend gate, because the 'ma' gate as written asks whether price is ABOVE its average -- the wrong condition for a short.

sweptAxes.axis: short side with a direction-aware trend gate
sweptAxes.result: The gate is now inverted for shorts in backtest.js, and it helps -- $816.25 against $633.27 ungated -- but every one of 72 configurations still loses over the full period.

chopFilter, requireHigherLow and minRoomR are ALL inert for breakout -- flagged automatically by sweep.mjs's inertAxes. Only trendGateMode and exitOnSwingHigh bind. Three more silent no-ops, bringing the total found to eight.

sweptAxes.axis: short side with the full exit engine
sweptAxes.result: Still loses in all 72 configurations. Best $816.25, a 18.4% loss, at a 49.38% drawdown -- identical to the best result before the exit engine was built. And lockBreakeven FALSE tops the table: the breakeven lock, which is worth a great deal on the long side, does nothing for the short side here.

leader.name: walk-forward-endorsed
leader.why: Every component chosen by a training-only search. btcRegime 50 is the newest: it had never actually been OFFERED to the walk-forward -- the filter grid held only null, atrPctBand and atrPctBand+crossSection -- and once offered it was chosen in nine quarters of nine, taking the out-of-sample result from $2300.28 at 13.39% to $2588.43 at 10.96%. Better on both axes in sample too, and it is the only change that has moved 2025.

readThisFirst: breakout + a 200-day MA trend gate is the first config to beat its own random-entry null by a detectable margin (p=0.005, excess 1.55R vs an MDE of 1.34R), and it does it at a 12.43% drawdown against BTC's 52.06%. It is still the best of 1152 in-sample configurations, so treat it as the thing to attack next, not as a finding. Everything before it -- long tpR, long maxHold -- was buying exposure in a rising market.
unsweptAxes: new filters not yet in backtest.js
nextUp: Untested cells remaining: CARRY (crypto funding rates, free from exchange APIs, the second-most documented factor and a genuinely different mechanism); CROSS-ASSET RANKING (crypto and equities in ONE universe, never done); and the equities-only factors need a third universe to decide whether they are asset-class-specific or simply spurious.

randomEntryNull.reading: The leader's entry rule is worth 0.0973R against a coin flip with identical geometry, and a random-entry account ends ABOVE it. No config's excess reaches what this test could detect, so the honest statement is not 'no edge' but 'no edge large enough to see through the noise a 100R target creates'.

breakout + ma200 gate (the leader).reading: The first configuration in this campaign whose excess over a matched-geometry random entry exceeds what the test can detect. It survives the harder version too: restricting the random entries to bars the 200-MA gate allows makes the excess LARGER, so the gate is not doing the work on its own. Caveat that has to stay attached: this is the best of ~1152 configurations searched on the same data, and at that many draws roughly 6 configs reach p<0.005 by chance. p=0.005 is not a discovery here, it is a reason to keep testing this one.

leveredLeader.reading: Not a better strategy, the same one levered 20x. A 94% drawdown means $1000 was worth about $60 at the low. Reported because the owner asked for the highest number; the drawdown is reported with it because the number is meaningless without it.

concentration.reading: 2025 lifts from +0.21R to +0.74R -- the only change in the campaign that has moved the worst year. The decay is reduced, not cured: 3.14 -> 2.05 -> 0.74 is still a decline, and 2026's five trades are negative.

walkForward.runner: walkforward.mjs (node walkforward.mjs, ~2 min), pinned by walkforward.test.mjs
walkForward.construction: Each quarter of 2024-01-01..2026-03-31 is scored by parameters fitted only on bars that closed before it began. Nine quarters chained into one curve.

inSampleComparison.reading: +1.85R in-sample against +1.14R out-of-sample over the identical window. That gap is the size of the hindsight, measured rather than guessed: roughly 40% of the apparent edge was the search seeing the answer.

walkForward.parameterStability: trendMa 150 and minStopPct 0.03 and volTarget 0.05 chosen in ALL NINE quarters; beTriggerR 2.5 in seven of nine. The search is not chasing noise. Note it never picks the full-sample leader's trendMa 200.
walkForward.quarterlyShape: Four of nine quarters positive. The return is concentrated in 2024Q1 (+2.84R), 2024Q4 (+1.73R) and 2025Q3 (+2.90R) -- the same fat-tail dependence as the in-sample result.
walkForward.leaksStillPresent: This is NOT a clean holdout and must not be quoted as one. The grid was designed after seeing full-sample results; the universe was chosen after seeing all of it; and walkforward.mjs's FIXED block holds the entry mode, the filters, and the one-bar fill delay constant at values selected in-sample rather than refitting them. Refitting those too would be the stronger test and has not been run.

laterStarts.reading: This is the caveat that matters most. The whole out-of-sample result is three quarters out of nine -- 2024Q1, 2024Q4 and 2025Q3. The other six are negative. Restricted to 2025 the walk-forward is positive ONLY because of 2025Q3; four of its five quarters lose money. A book running this would have spent most of its time losing and made everything back in three quarters. That is the trade-level tail dependence showing up at the quarter level, and it is what trend following is -- but it means nobody should read $1974.68 as a steady climb.

refitEverything.what: Entry mode, fill delay and filters refitted every quarter alongside the numeric parameters, instead of held at in-sample values. 576 configs x 9 quarters.
refitEverything.vsRestricted: Better than the $1974.68 of the version that held those three constant. Removing the leak did not cost anything -- it helped.

whatItChose.entryDelayBars 1: ALL NINE quarters, on training data alone. The one-bar fill delay was not an in-sample spike; an independent search picks it every time.
whatItChose.entryMode breakout: eight of nine (anticipate once, in 2024Q2, which lost)
whatItChose.filters null: SEVEN OF NINE. A training-only search mostly DECLINES the filters, which confirms what the in-sample sweeps only hinted: they are noise, not signal.

refitEverything.stillFixed: What remains held at in-sample values is the structural frame, and it is not nothing: long-only, trendGate on in 'ma' mode, tpR 100, maxStopPct 0.20, alignMode none, lockBreakeven on, beLockR 0.2, volClamp 3. The trend gate in particular was chosen in-sample and is the single change that created this result.
refitEverything.quarterlyShape: Four of nine positive: 2024Q1 +2.84R, 2024Q3 +0.22R, 2024Q4 +3.53R, 2025Q3 +1.11R. The other five negative. Same concentration as every other cut of this result.

structuralRefit.what: Refit the structural frame too -- whether to gate at all, in which mode, and the target multiple -- not just the tuned numbers. 384 configs x 9 quarters.
structuralRefit.vsEarlier: Best walk-forward yet: $1974.68 (numbers only) -> $2249.27 (+ entry mode, delay, filters) -> $2300.28 (+ the structural frame). Every leak closed so far has made the result better, not worse.

whatItChose.tpR 100: eight of nine (tpR 12 once, in 2024Q2, which lost)

structuralRefit.reading: This is the strongest evidence in the campaign. A search that has never seen the quarter it is judged on converges on the same structure nine times out of nine -- INCLUDING on whether to apply the trend gate at all, which was the one choice most obviously made with hindsight. The gate is not an in-sample artifact.
structuralRefit.stillFixed: long-only, entryMode breakout, entryDelayBars 1, filters null, alignMode none (inert), maxStopPct 0.20, lockBreakeven, beLockR 0.2, volClamp 3. The first three were each chosen independently in 8/9 or 9/9 quarters by the previous refit, so holding them is now a recorded observation rather than an assumption.

fittingObjective.why: The walk-forward's fit function maximised final balance and nothing else. Given a choice between an unlimited book and one capped at three positions it took unlimited in all nine quarters, because more concurrent bets is more balance in-sample -- it never saw that unlimited got there through a 24% drawdown while the cap took 9%. The campaign's leader had been picked on drawdown TOO, so the walk-forward was being asked to validate a choice made on a criterion it did not share.
fittingObjective.fix: walkforward.mjs now takes objective 'balance' or 'mar' (balance per unit of drawdown). Both are reported.

mar.chose: maxConcurrent 2 @0.5% for four quarters, then unlimited @1% for five

fittingObjective.conclusion: The concurrency cap is NOT validated out of sample under either objective. Its large in-sample gain was hindsight.

btcRegimeOffered.chose: btcRegime 50 in nine quarters of nine under the balance objective, eight of nine under mar
btcRegimeOffered.progression: $1974.68 (numbers only) -> $2249.27 (+ entry mode, delay, filters) -> $2300.28 (+ structural frame) -> $2588.43 (+ btcRegime offered). Every step improved it.
btcRegimeOffered.lessonRecorded: The filters were reported as 'declined in 7 of 9 quarters'. That was true of the filters the grid CONTAINED. btcRegime alone was never in it. A component absent from a grid is not a component the search rejected, and the write-up did not distinguish those.

gridSizeIsAVariable.ladder: Four grid sizes, same fixed frame, same window, trendMa pinned at 150 so grid size is the only thing that varies.
gridSizeIsAVariable.finding: Grid size matters and there is an INTERIOR optimum, around eight points here. Eight beats two and it beats forty-eight and one hundred and ninety-two, on balance, drawdown and mean R alike.
gridSizeIsAVariable.correction: The previous commit claimed 'a bigger honest grid is a worse grid'. That is too strong and is withdrawn. It rested on one comparison, $2588.43 against $2387.26, which was partly confounded -- the small grid pinned trendMa at 150 while the large one swept it. With the confound removed the relationship is not monotone: 192 points beats 48, and 2 points loses to 8. The direction of the original observation survives for grids above the optimum; the general claim does not.
gridSizeIsAVariable.stabilityHypothesisRefuted: Choice stability, computed from training runs alone, does NOT rank grids. It flags the worst one -- medium at 0.778 -- but tiny and small both score a perfect 1.000 and differ by 13% in out-of-sample balance. It is a useful warning sign and not a selection criterion, and it was proposed here as the latter.
gridSizeIsAVariable.consequenceForTheLeader: None. The leader already comes from the eight-point grid, which the corrected ladder confirms is the best of the four.

bugsFound.symptom: reported -0.42R and $883.39 out of sample -- a clean negative result
bugsFound.cause: each quarter's run was truncated at the quarter end, amputating every position still open when the quarter closed. With 50-to-200-bar holds that is most of them, and the amputated part is the tail that carries a trend follower's return.
bugsFound.caught: by checking the same configurations held FIXED over the identical window, which scored +0.74R to +1.85R. A -0.42R result next to a +1.85R result for the same trades is not a finding, it is a bug.
bugsFound.fix: exits now run to the end of the data; only ENTRY dates are confined to the decision window. Letting a trade run its course after entry is not lookahead -- its exit rule was fixed when it was entered. Pinned by a test.

bugsFound.symptom: a nine-quarter refit of eight axes printed as though only five had been fitted
bugsFound.cause: `chose` was a hardcoded list of five keys rather than derived from the grid
bugsFound.impact: whether the entry mode and filters moved between quarters -- the entire question that run existed to answer -- was invisible in its own output
bugsFound.fix: chose is now derived from Object.keys(grid); pinned by a test

bugsFound.symptom: a sweep of four btcRegime periods returned four byte-identical rows for the short side
bugsFound.cause: entryGate was wired into the anticipate branch and the shared dip/breakout branch but not into bos, so every filters spec was silently ignored for that entry mode
bugsFound.fix: entryGate is now checked in all three branches and its refusals are tallied as reason externalGate; a test asserts a gate that refuses everything produces no trades in bos, breakout and anticipate alike

bugsFound.symptom: would have admitted shorts only into rising markets
bugsFound.cause: 'BTC above its own average' is a market-wide uptrend, applied unchanged to both directions -- the same bug class as backtest.js's trend gate
bugsFound.fix: direction-aware, with a test covering both directions against both a rising and a falling BTC

bugsFound.symptom: eight parameters accepted and silently ignored, each producing byte-identical rows that read as a swept axis
bugsFound.list: stopMode outside anticipate; alignMode outside bos/anticipate; the swing window for breakout; trailStartR below trailR; entryGate in the bos branch; chopFilter, requireHigherLow and minRoomR for breakout
bugsFound.fix: A capability table now declares which entry modes honour alignMode, chopFilter, requireHigherLow and minRoomR, and passing a RESTRICTIVE value to a mode that ignores it throws. Permissive values never throw -- alignMode 'none' asks for no alignment, which is exactly what an ignoring mode delivers, so it drops no claim and the whole campaign passes it. The signature default is accepted everywhere too, because omission and an explicit default cannot be told apart.

bugsFound.symptom: reported that stability does not predict performance AND that bigger grids do better -- the opposite of the previous commit
bugsFound.cause: trendMa was not in the ladder's FIXED block, so the two grids that did not SWEEP it fell back to backtest.js's default of 20 instead of the endorsed 150. The ladder measured 'was trendMa fitted at all', not grid size.
bugsFound.caught: the two smallest grids scoring far below every walk-forward already recorded, which no change in grid size could explain
bugsFound.fix: trendMa pinned at 150 in FIXED, with a comment saying why; ladder re-run

bugsFound.symptom: every equities file ended with the live session's incomplete row — real timestamp and OHL, empty close
bugsFound.cause: the loader only validated `time`; parseFloat("") is NaN and every NaN comparison is false, so that bar would trigger neither a stop nor a target and simply be stepped over
bugsFound.fix: bars with any non-finite OHLC are dropped, with a test built from the real failing shape

bugsFound.symptom: CANDLE_COST_MODEL was set correctly and the first equities run still died saying no cost model was named
bugsFound.cause: the env fallback lived in the signature default, and a JS default parameter only fires on `undefined` — every call site passes `config.x ?? null`, so both env vars were unreachable through the harness
bugsFound.fix: resolved inside the function body; tests pin the null-call-site path for both

concurrency.measured: The unlimited book peaks at 19 simultaneous positions on 2024-12-03 and spends 26% of its time with 9 or more open. It is flat 20.4% of the time.
concurrency.whyItMatters: simulateEquity compounds trades one after another in entry order, which silently assumes the book is never long two things at once. It is. Sequential compounding cannot see correlated positions moving together, so every drawdown this campaign reported before this point is a FLOOR, not a measurement. maxConcurrent does not fix the accounting -- it constrains the book the way a real one is constrained, and declined signals are counted and reported rather than quietly dropped.
concurrency.stillUnmodelled: Positions are still compounded sequentially rather than marked to market together, so a correlated multi-position drawdown is still not directly measured.

equitiesBlocked.status: Cannot be tested in this container. Outbound HTTPS to public market-data hosts is denied by the environment's network policy -- the proxy gateway answers 403 to CONNECT for stooq.com and stooq.pl, confirmed in its own status endpoint.
equitiesBlocked.whatWouldUnblockIt: Equities daily bars supplied the same way the crypto bundle was: a tar.gz of per-symbol CSVs with time,open,high,low,close,volume. bundle-loader.mjs reads that format already and nothing else would need to change.
equitiesBlocked.whyItMatters: The owner named equities as the actual target. FINDINGS.md's own equities section is a warning about this exact failure mode -- an apparent edge that turned out to be the window's payoff geometry.

decayDiagnosis.question: Is the leader's decline (2023 +2.92R, 2024 +2.01R, 2025 +0.21R, 2026 -0.94R) the strategy dying or the market going quiet?
decayDiagnosis.answer: BOTH, and that is a better answer than either alone. What a RANDOM long entry earned under the same geometry fell from +0.76R to -0.86R -- no strategy choice can explain that, the trend simply stopped being there. But the strategy's EXCESS over random fell too, from +2.16R to +0.27R to -0.08R. So the market got harder AND the edge over a coin flip shrank.
decayDiagnosis.theSharpPoint: In 2025 the strategy beat a random entry by 0.27R. The campaign's own power analysis puts the smallest excess this test can detect at roughly 1.3-1.5R. In 2025 the strategy is not distinguishable from a coin flip.
decayDiagnosis.notAnArtefact: Checked at stop widths of 4%, 6%, 10% and 15%. The level of the random-entry return moves; the year ordering never does.
decayDiagnosis.sideNote: The efficiency ratio barely moved (0.171 to 0.146, a 17% range). What collapsed was the DIRECTION of the moves, not their straightness -- 2025-26 crypto was no choppier, it just stopped going up.

shortSide.fullPeriod: Loses in all 99 configurations swept. Best $816.25, a 18.4% loss, at a 49.38% drawdown.
shortSide.theInterestingPart: Shorts are POSITIVE in 2024 and 2025 -- 2025 being exactly the year the long side collapsed to +0.21R. The two sides are complementary in time.

combined.verdict: Combining makes it worse on both axes. The short side's 2023 losses (-0.50R over 110 trades) outweigh its 2024-25 gains.

shortSide.theHandicapThatMattersAndIsNotResolved: The engine implements shorts for entryMode 'bos' only and on the base stop/target/timeout path alone -- no breakeven lock, no trailing stop, no partials. The long side's result depends materially on the breakeven lock (beTriggerR 3, chosen by the walk-forward in nine quarters of nine), so the short side is being judged with a worse exit engine than the long side. The measured gap is far too large for the lock to close (-18% against +1575%), so the conclusion 'shorts do not rescue this' stands -- but 'shorts do not work' is NOT established and would need the short exit path built first.
shortSide.engineChange: backtest.js's trend gate is now direction-aware. Both gate conditions describe an uptrend; applied unchanged to a short they permitted selling only into rising markets, which is worse than no gate at all. Two tests pin both directions.
shortSide.engineNowComplete: trailR, trailStartR, partialAtR, partialFrac, trailingTpPct, lockBreakeven and exitOnSwingHigh are all mirrored for shorts. Only two ENTRY-side conditions remain long-only and they are genuinely unwritten rather than untested: requireHigherLow (a rising sequence of swing lows) and minRoomR (clear air above entry, measured by a nearestResAbove with no nearestSupportBelow counterpart).
shortSide.verdictUpgraded: Previously recorded as 'shorts do not rescue this, but shorts do not work is NOT established' because the short side was being judged with a worse exit engine. It is now judged with the same one and the answer does not move: the short side loses on this data. The handicap was not the explanation.
shortSide.whyItStillMattered: The engine capability is the deliverable. The owner wants the short path for EQUITIES, where a two-sided book is the normal construction rather than an afterthought.

equitiesReadiness.formatGivenToOwner: candle-bundle/1440/<SYMBOL>.csv, header time,open,high,low,close,volume, time in unix seconds, oldest row first. bundle-loader.mjs reads it unchanged.
equitiesReadiness.whatWasHardcoded: Three call sites assumed XBTUSD was the market: benchmark.mjs's headline row, campaign.mjs's btcRegime series, and robustness.mjs's copy of it. On an equities bundle the benchmark would have printed 'BTC $n/a' next to every leaderboard and the btcRegime filter would have refused to compile with a message about BTC. Two of the three would have gone quiet, which is how the other eight silent no-ops in this campaign got as far as they did.
equitiesReadiness.fix: bundle-loader.marketProxy resolves it from the universe against an ordered candidate list -- XBTUSD, SPY, VOO, IVV, ^GSPC, QQQ -- honours an explicit override or CANDLE_MARKET_PROXY, and THROWS when it cannot resolve, naming what it looked for. benchmarks() now returns proxySymbol/proxy/proxyMaxDrawdownPct instead of btc/btcMaxDrawdownPct, because a field called 'btc' on an equities run is a lie even when the number is right.
stillToDoWhenDataArrives: declare survivorship bias unless the bundle demonstrably includes delisted names
confirm with the owner whether prices are split/dividend adjusted -- adjustment changes historical stop distances, and stop distance is the variable this whole campaign turned on
rename btcRegime to marketRegime once it is used on a second asset class
runOrder: robustness.mjs with the crypto-fitted leader untouched (the honest transfer test)
walkforward.mjs with an EIGHT-point grid (the corrected ladder's optimum)
only then sweep, and stop early

costModel.built: costs.mjs. Named models with sourced numbers: krakenTaker (0.008/0.0005, what every crypto result here was computed under), usEquityRetail (0/0.0005), usEquityIbkr (0.00005/0.0005), and zeroCost as a labelled diagnostic.
costModel.whyItRefusesToGuess: A crypto universe defaults to krakenTaker so existing results stay reproducible. Anything else must be named. The failure mode of guessing is not a slightly wrong number: at a 3% stop crypto pays 0.57R a trade and US equities pay 0.033R, so equities charged Kraken rates would look like a dead strategy and crypto charged equity rates would manufacture an edge. costFor() throws on an unrecognised universe and the message says so.
costModel.identity: costInR(model, stopPct) = 2*(feeRate+slipPct)/stopPct. Pinned by a test against the two figures the campaign turned on: 1.70R at a 1% stop, 0.11R at 15%.
costModel.verified: The leader reproduces byte-identically after the rewiring -- 182 trades, $20,949.34, 20.77%.

equities.bundle: equity-bundle/1440, 30 symbols (10 sector/index ETFs + 20 large caps), 920 daily bars each, 2023-01-03 to 2026-09-02. Raw unadjusted OHLC from yfinance via Colab. Held in a SEPARATE root from candle-bundle so the two universes can never be mixed.
equities.costModel: usEquityRetail — 0 commission, 5bp per-leg slippage. Named explicitly; costFor() refused to run until it was.

transferTest.what: The crypto-fitted leader, not one parameter changed, run on equities.

THE_RESULT.reading: $15,873 is the UNIVERSE, not the strategy. A random entry on the same 30 symbols with the same stop distances, target, hold and cost earns 0.5751R against the strategy's 0.5814R. The excess is 0.0064R at p=0.47 -- a coin flip. It fails the harder gated-bar version too. Thirty of today's mega caps and sector ETFs over 2023-2026 make money almost however you enter them; the equal-weight basket alone returns $2,646.
THE_RESULT.whyTheDollarsMislead: A random-entry ACCOUNT computed as 1000*(1+0.01*0.5751)^252 lands near $4,242, which invites the reading that the strategy's $15,873 beat it. It does not: that formula is a crude geometric approximation with no volatility targeting and no path ordering, so it is not like-for-like. The rigorous comparison is mean R per trade, and there the two are the same number.

equities.selectionBiasConfirmed: This was flagged as a caveat before the run and the null turned it into the explanation. The symbol list was 30 currently-listed large caps chosen by me — NVDA at $15,676 buy-and-hold is in it and the companies that failed are not. Survivorship-free equities data (Norgate, Sharadar, CRSP) is the only way to test this properly and it is a paid source.

subgroupDiagnostic.whyItIsWorthRunning: The matched-geometry null draws from the same symbols in the same proportions, so it already controls for the universe being a basket of winners. That conclusion -- no detectable edge -- stands on its own and survivorship does not undermine it. What survivorship DOES remove is the thing a trend gate is for: the chance to avoid a name that falls and keeps falling.
subgroupDiagnostic.reading: Directionally consistent: on names that only rose, the strategy is WORSE than random -- its stop-outs are pure drag. On the laggards, random entry earns almost nothing (+0.0225R) and the strategy earns +0.3871R.
whyItIsNotAFinding: the excess of 0.3646R is BELOW the 0.696R this test could detect at 80% power
the split is POST-HOC -- subgroups defined by an outcome only knowable at the end, so it is not tradeable as stated
two subgroups tested, so even the nominal p carries a multiplicity cost
subgroupDiagnostic.prereg: EQUITIES-LAGGARD-EXCESS-2026-09, registry ledger seq 15, registered before any survivorship-free data exists so the prediction cannot be reshaped once it does.

survivorshipFreeRoute.correction: Recorded because it was stated the other way earlier: a survivorship-free universe was called a paid product. Partly wrong. The bulk of the reconstruction is free and mechanical; only the departed names are.
survivorshipFreeRoute.whatWorks: Wikipedia's constituents table carries a Date-added column, so every current member that JOINED after 2023-01-01 is removed by rule -- roughly sixty companies that entered the index because they did well. No judgement involved.
survivorshipFreeRoute.whatDoesNot: The 'Selected changes' table that listed REMOVALS is gone from that page. Verified 2026-09-04: it returns two tables and the second is a navbox. So the departed names are hand-supplied from recall, the list is incomplete, and its incompleteness is the residual survivorship bias. The manifest reports how many resolved, which bounds what got in but not what was never listed.
survivorshipFreeRoute.standing: Better than a hand-picked basket of winners, worse than a vendor point-in-time file. Results must be labelled that way and not called survivorship-free.
survivorshipFreeRoute.debugHistory: Three scripts failed before this one and the useful lesson is about diagnosis, not Wikipedia: v1 and v2 used a `!pip` cell magic that is a SyntaxError when the file is run rather than pasted, so nothing executed and nothing printed -- a silent failure indistinguishable from several other causes. v3 removed the magic and printed a checkpoint per step, which located the real fault in one run.

acceptanceCriterion.asStated: ~10 trades a month, win rate at or above 40%, wins large enough to offset the losses.
acceptanceCriterion.met: Yes, on every count, by the current equities candidate: 5.7 trades/month, 40.5% win rate, 2.92R average win against a 1.01R average loss, expectancy +0.5814R.
acceptanceCriterion.andAlsoMetBy: A RANDOM ENTRY using the same exits: 42.8% win rate -- HIGHER than the strategy -- with a 2.67 payoff and +0.5589R expectancy. That is the whole problem with the criterion as an acceptance test.
acceptanceCriterion.whyTheShapeIsFree: A wide stop with no reachable take-profit and a bounded hold caps the loss near 1R and lets winners run past 3R. A ~40% win rate at a ~2.7 payoff is therefore a property of the EXIT geometry, not the entry, and it comes free with any long entry in a rising market. Breakeven at a 2.89:1 payoff is a 25.7% win rate, so 40% clears it with room -- and so does the coin flip's 42.8%.

whatFrequencyCosts.reading: Low frequency does not reduce risk, it buys noise. Ten trades a month needs about three years to confirm a half-R edge and over a decade for a quarter-R one, before any allowance for same-day clustering.

failed.sample_sufficient: effective n 175 against 882 required to detect a quarter-R edge

gateVerdict.reading: Four conditions green including the owner's own criterion. It fails on the two that decide whether the result is real.

THE_ANSWER.question: Does the trend-gated breakout entry carry an edge over a matched random entry?
THE_ANSWER.answer: No, in either asset class, and the last remaining hypothesis is refuted rather than merely unproven.
THE_ANSWER.crypto: 29 pairs, 2,446 configurations. Best out-of-sample $2,588 at 11.0% drawdown against BTC's $4,106 at 52%.
THE_ANSWER.equities30: Excess +0.0064R, p=0.4741. The $15,873 was the universe: a coin flip with the same exits earned 0.5751R against 0.5814R.

equities128.reading: The registered prediction was that the strategy adds value by declining to hold falling names. It does the opposite: WORSE than random on the losers, monotonically worse the weaker the name. The +0.3646R laggard excess on the 30-symbol bundle was noise and reversed sign on four times the sample.

THE_ANSWER.prereg: EQUITIES-LAGGARD-EXCESS-2026-09 linked at ledger seq 16, verdict FAIL. Ledger verifies at 17 entries.
THE_ANSWER.whatIsNotInDoubt: The payoff geometry works and is free: ~40% win rate at a ~2.9 payoff, positive expectancy, confidence interval excluding zero. The owner's acceptance criterion is met in full. A coin flip meets it too, which is why it cannot be the acceptance test.
THE_ANSWER.revisedBy: crossSectionalMomentum below. The earlier answer was correct about ENTRY TIMING and wrong as a general claim, because every null this project had built was blind to selection.

sp500Bundle.whatArrived: 129 symbols from the hand-assembled list, no manifest -- the simple script was run, not the Wikipedia reconstruction. SBNY dropped as a reused ticker (515 bars from 2024-08-15; the bank failed 2023-03). 128 used.
sp500Bundle.yahooDropsDelistedNames: The decisive data finding, contradicting an assertion made earlier in this session: Yahoo serves essentially no delisted history. Of ten delisted names attempted -- SIVB, FRC, PACW, DISH, CTLT, PXD, MRO, WBA, CMA, IPG -- zero usable series were obtained. The free route cannot produce a survivorship-free universe; the membership reconstruction is free, the prices are not.
sp500Bundle.whyTheResultStillStands: 38 symbols lost money buy-and-hold (30%, against 7% in the first bundle) including CHPT -97%, LCID -92%, SEDG -88%, ENPH -86%. The hypothesis had ample population to show itself in and showed the opposite.
sp500Bundle.rawPriceArtifacts: Unadjusted prices carry split discontinuities: MRNA +177% in a day, CHPT +75% on the final bar. auto_adjust=False preserves stop distances at that cost -- a tradeoff not stated when the advice was given.

crossSectionalMomentum.whyItWasNeverTested: Every test before this asked whether ENTRY TIMING beats random, and matchedGeometryNull answers that by drawing random entries FROM THE SAME SYMBOLS IN THE SAME PROPORTIONS. That design holds symbol selection constant, so it is blind BY CONSTRUCTION to an edge living in WHICH asset you hold rather than WHEN you buy. Cross-sectional momentum is exactly that kind of edge and is among the most replicated results in the literature (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993, still present in their 2023 follow-up; time-series momentum with post-crisis Sharpe comparable to pre-2008, Moskowitz/Ooi/Pedersen and Baltas/Kosowski 2020).
crossSectionalMomentum.theRule: At each monthly rebalance, rank every symbol by its return over the past 252 bars skipping the most recent 21, hold the top decile equally weighted. No stop, no target, no entry trigger.
crossSectionalMomentum.parametersArePreSpecified: 252 formation / 21 skip / 21 rebalance / top decile is the canonical Jegadeesh-Titman construction from 1993, not a configuration selected from a sweep. That matters: it is not best-of-N.
crossSectionalMomentum.nullThatMatters: Random SELECTION -- pick topK uniformly from the same eligible set at each rebalance and hold identically. It isolates the ranking, which is the only thing the strategy does.
crossSectionalMomentum.lookbackPattern: Structured rather than scattered: every 252-bar configuration beats random (p=0.0149, 0.0199) and every 126-bar configuration fails (p=0.61, 0.93, 1.00). Short lookbacks getting eaten by reversal is what the literature predicts, which is weak evidence the effect is real rather than fitted.
whatIsNotEstablished: The three universes are NOT independent -- same 2023-2026 regime, and sp500-128 contains the equities-30 symbols. The p-values must not be combined.
It beats SPY over the identical window by only 5.7% ($1743 against $1649) at a worse drawdown, 29.7% against ~21%. Risk-adjusted against the index it is close to a wash.
Crypto's 66.96% drawdown makes that version untradeable as constructed.
Only 2.66 years of rotation after the 252-bar warmup: roughly 32 rebalances.
No walk-forward yet, and no promotion-gate run.
crossSectionalMomentum.correctnessChecks: xsmom.test.mjs, 7 tests, including one that fails on look-ahead: a symbol that only rises AFTER the rebalance must not be selected. Ranking is by DATE across a shared calendar, not by bar index, so symbols starting on different dates are never compared out of period.

1_concentration_LONG_ONLY.result: BAD. 31 monthly periods; the best 3 produce 96.8% of the total return, the best single month 43%. 61% of months positive. Same fragility as every earlier finding.
1_concentration_LONG_ONLY.verdict: the long-only rotation is a tail-dependent result like everything before it

3_longShort.reading: The ranking genuinely separates: the bottom decile loses a third a year. The dollar-neutral spread beats SPY ($1649) at HALF its drawdown -- 9.91% against ~21% -- and concentration falls from 96.8% to 44.5%. This is the first result in the project that is simultaneously better AND less fragile.

3b_borrowStress.reading: At realistic borrow (2-10%) the spread holds 26-31% CAGR at ~10% drawdown against SPY's ~20% at 21%. It only degrades to index-like at 30%+ borrow, which is exceptional rather than typical.

attacks.survivorshipNowFavoursTheResult: A reversal worth stating: for the long-only entry work, missing delisted names INFLATED results. For a long-short, they DEFLATE it. SIVB and FRC went to zero and would have sat in the bottom decile paying the short leg. Their absence from this bundle makes the spread an understatement.

4_walkForward.construction: Parameters (lookback, topK) refit each quarter from a six-point grid using only bars that closed before that quarter. Skip and rebalance held at the canonical 21/21 -- refitting those would turn a literature-specified strategy into a search result.
4_walkForward.parameterStability: 252/5 chosen in ALL SEVEN quarters. The canonical lookback every time.
4_walkForward.reading: Every earlier result in this project lost about 40% of its apparent edge to a walk-forward and one lost all of it. This one lost nothing: 35.1% CAGR out of sample at a 10.4% drawdown against SPY's 18.6% over the identical window, with perfectly stable parameter selection.

spreadReplication.reading: Two strong, one weak, and the weak one is explained rather than anomalous: the 30-name bundle is all winners -- only 7% of it lost money -- so its bottom decile still ROSE and the short leg had nothing to work with. The spread needs dispersion and delivers where dispersion exists. Crypto is the striking case: a 67%-drawdown long strategy becomes a 9%-drawdown spread with a higher balance.

whatRemainsUnproven: 20 out-of-sample monthly periods, 1.61 years, one market regime. That is the binding limitation and no amount of further analysis on this data fixes it.
No live or paper trading. Nothing here has met a real spread or a real borrow desk.
Short availability is modelled as a flat borrow rate. In practice parts of the bottom decile are hard to borrow or unborrowable, and that is lumpy rather than uniform.
Yahoo serves no delisted history, so the bundles contain no failures. For a LONG-SHORT this understates rather than flatters -- the failures would have paid the short leg -- but it is still a gap.
The three universes overlap in period and partly in symbols; their p-values must not be combined.

spreadNull.construction: Draw 2*topK symbols uniformly, split them arbitrarily into a long half and a short half, run the same dollar-neutral book. Asks the only question worth asking of a spread: does RANKING the two sides beat splitting the same names at random?
spreadNull.reading: The spread sits entirely outside the null distribution -- above its 95th percentile. The cleanest null result the project has produced.

gateVerdict.unitCaveat: promotion.mjs was written for per-trade R-multiples and a rotation has no stop and therefore no R. Monthly spread log returns are used instead, one per rebalance, and every threshold is read in those units.

failed.sample_sufficient: effective n 31 against 32 required -- short by one period
failed.beats_baseline_controls: mean monthly 0.02150 against SPY's 0.02251. ON RAW RETURN, SPY BEATS THE SPREAD over the full window.

gateVerdict.blockedPermanently: pre_registration. Registering a hypothesis after seeing its result is not pre-registration; BLOCKED here is correct and must not be filled in retrospectively.
gateVerdict.theHonestReading: Seven conditions pass including the two hardest -- the matched null and out-of-sample replication. The baseline failure is real and is the thing to understand: this is a RISK-ADJUSTED improvement, not a raw-return one. Return per unit of drawdown is 2.92 against SPY's 0.89, but unlevered the spread returns less than simply owning the index over this window.

riskMatchedComparison.why: A market-neutral book at a 10% drawdown is not comparable to an index at 21% until the risk is matched. Financing charged at 6% annualised on the borrowed portion.
riskMatchedComparison.whatThisDoesNotSay: Leverage is a separate decision with its own failure modes -- margin calls, financing that moves against you, and gap risk that a monthly rebalance cannot react to. The risk-matched number answers the gate's raw-return objection; it does not make 2x a recommendation. And it multiplies the momentum-crash exposure, which is the strategy's known failure mode and is absent from this sample.

CORRECTION_drawdown.what: Every spread drawdown reported before 2026-09-04T14:00 was understated by about 44%.
CORRECTION_drawdown.cause: spread() combined MONTHLY period returns, so the drawdown was sampled only at rebalance points and never saw an intra-month low.
CORRECTION_drawdown.caughtBy: multifactor.runBook, an independent implementation that marks every bar, disagreeing with spread() on the same configuration.
CORRECTION_drawdown.secondErrorDuringTheFix: The first fix took the BALANCE from the per-bar path too, which silently dropped turnover and slippage (charged at rebalances) and inflated the result 9%, from $1947.50 to $2130.88. Balance now comes from the costed monthly path and drawdown from a per-bar walk anchored to it.
CORRECTION_drawdown.nowCrossChecked: spread() and runBook agree within $5.49 and 0.02 drawdown points on the same configuration.
CORRECTION_drawdown.whatItChanges: The claim 'half of SPY's drawdown' was wrong. 14.55% against SPY's ~21% is better, not half. The gate's survivable condition still passes at 14.55 against a 25 ceiling. Nothing else in the verdict moves.

threeVariations.designedTo: occupy DIFFERENT cells of the edge space so they can fail independently, rather than re-parameterise the winner

V1_timeSeriesFilter.cell: whether to be in at all
V1_timeSeriesFilter.result: WORSE everywhere. sp500 $882 (CAGR -4.8%) against baseline $1942; crypto $1617 against $2834.

V2_multiHorizon.result: WORSE. sp500 $1409, crypto $1342. Averaging ranks across 21/63/126/252 dilutes rather than confirms.

V3_volScaled.result: WORSE on return, much better on drawdown: sp500 $1309 at 6.56% DD, crypto $1394 at 9.1%. But risk-adjusted it still loses -- 1.68 return-per-drawdown against the baseline's 2.01.

threeVariations.combinations: All seven combinations underperform the baseline on both universes.
threeVariations.reading: A clean negative and worth as much as the positive. The canonical 1993 construction beat all three of my improvements on both universes. That is evidence the original is not a lucky parameterisation -- deviations from it in three independent directions all cost money.

crossSectionalMomentum.calendarBugCheck: Checked against the same bug and CLEAN: this section's crypto CAGR of 36.03% on a $2430.28 final implies 2.886 years, which is the true span, so its year count was never the assumed n/12. Its 66.96% drawdown is a per-bar figure from the rotation curve, not a period-end mark.

factorBattery.why: 'Test everything' and 'report an honest result' are in tension and the tension is arithmetic. Twelve signals at p<0.05 produce 0.6 false positives by expectation. Every signal is scored against the same null with the same machinery and corrected together with Benjamini-Hochberg.
factorBattery.signals: momentum, reversal1m, reversal1w, lowVol, highVol, nearHigh, trendQuality, acceleration, lowSkew, volumeTrend, idioVol, beta -- each a documented anomaly, so the battery is a replication attempt rather than a fishing expedition.

equities128.note: five signals hit p=0.0050, the floor with 200 draws

factorBattery.correlationFinding: The six equities survivors are TWO factors, not six. A momentum cluster (momentum, nearHigh, trendQuality) correlates 0.78-0.91 internally; a low-risk cluster (lowVol, idioVol, beta) correlates 0.79-0.87 internally; and momentum against lowVol is only 0.22. BH assumes independence and these are strongly positively dependent, so 'six survivors of twelve' overstates what was found.

replicatesOnBoth: nearHigh (p=0.005 both, but r=0.83 with momentum -- the same factor)
beta (p=0.020 equities, 0.010 crypto, weak and with a 40.5% crypto drawdown)
equitiesOnly: idioVol -- the BEST equities factor at 42.31% CAGR, collapses to -9.02% on crypto at p=0.83
crossAssetVerdict.reading: This is what the battery was for. Six equities survivors reduce to essentially ONE robust factor -- momentum, with nearHigh as its correlated proxy -- once a second asset class is required. The low-risk cluster that produced the best equities numbers does not survive the crossing, which is exactly the failure mode a single-universe battery would have reported as a discovery.

combination.note: Combining lowers drawdown below either leg (7.47%) because the two are only 0.22 correlated. But idioVol is equities-only, so this combination is not available cross-asset.

factorBattery.caveatOnSharpe: Sharpe 2.31 on 31 monthly observations has a standard error near 0.34. These are not precise numbers.

disjointHalvesAdjudication.why: The cross-asset crossing could not adjudicate idioVol, lowVol and trendQuality: they pass on sp500-128 and fail on crypto, and there is no third asset class to break the tie. This does not need one. Split the 128 equities into two disjoint halves and rank INSIDE each. A cross-sectional factor is a claim about RELATIVE ranking and must appear in both halves; a result carried by a handful of names appears in the half holding them and vanishes from the other.
disjointHalvesAdjudication.construction: Deterministic shuffle fixed before any result was seen, 64 + 64, topK 5 a side, 2000 null draws per half so the p floor is 0.0005 rather than the 0.0050 that five signals had been sitting on.

failsTheSplit.lowVol: p=0.0950 in half A against 0.0005 in half B -- and lowVol was the second-best equities number in the original battery.
failsTheSplit.volumeTrend: p=0.0415 / 0.9270, a sign flip between arbitrary halves of the same universe.

disjointHalvesAdjudication.whatItSettles: The low-risk cluster was three signals and is now one. idioVol survives at the p floor in BOTH halves, so its 42% equities CAGR is not a few names -- it is a real cross-sectional effect in equities that simply does not exist in crypto. lowVol and beta were riding on their correlation with it (0.79-0.87 internally) and do not stand alone. trendQuality also survives, though it correlates 0.78-0.91 with momentum and is likely the same factor wearing a different name.
disjointHalvesAdjudication.theNumberThatShouldWorry: Half A returns $1490.73 for idioVol and half B returns $3757.73. Same signal, same period, same construction, 2.5x apart on an ARBITRARY split of one universe. Every dollar figure in this campaign should be read against that spread: the sign and the significance replicate, the magnitude is close to meaningless at this sample size.
disjointHalvesAdjudication.whatItDoesNotSettle: The two halves share a period, a market and a macro regime, so they are not independent draws. Surviving the split rules out the few-names explanation. It does not touch the one-regime explanation, which remains the largest unaddressed risk in every result here.

rerunAt3000Draws.why: At 200 draws the smallest p a signal can report is 1/201 = 0.0050 and five equities signals sat exactly there, which says 'not resolved', not 'p = 0.005'. Re-run at 3000 draws (floor 3.33e-4) on the calendar-fixed and cost-fixed code. The null does not depend on the signal, so it is computed once and shared across the family -- which also makes explicit that all twelve p-values are read off the SAME null sample and are dependent by construction.
rerunAt3000Draws.stillAtTheFloor: Five equities signals and four crypto signals report 3.33e-4, which is again the floor. They never once lost to 3000 random draws. The honest statement is p < 3.3e-4, not p = 3.3e-4; more draws would only push the bound down.

equities128.note: beta scrapes in at p=1.47e-2 against a BH critical of 0.025.

crypto28.whatTheCostFixDidHere: The crypto null median fell from $932.54 to $508.58 once the short leg was charged. A random split turns over close to 100% of the book every rebalance against a ranked book's 25%, so the null was the larger beneficiary of the credit. Correcting it made the crypto signals look MORE significant, not less -- six survivors where the buggy run gave three. This is the concrete case of the general point: every p-value published before the cost fix was conservative.

threeFiltersInSequence.andThenCorrelation: Those three correlate 0.78 to 0.91 with each other. They are ONE factor with three names. Twelve documented anomalies, three independent screens, and what is left standing is cross-sectional momentum -- which is what the literature says, and is the outcome a battery should produce when it is working rather than fishing.
threeFiltersInSequence.idioVolIsTheOneRealSPLIT: idioVol passes equities BH at the floor and passes BOTH disjoint halves at the floor, so it is not a few names. It fails crypto outright at p=0.539 with a -21.6% CAGR. That is a genuine asset-class-specific factor rather than a spurious one, and it is the best equities number in the battery. It should be traded as an equities factor or not at all.
threeFiltersInSequence.whatTheHalvesTestCulledThatBHDidNot: lowVol and beta both survive BH on both universes and both FAIL the disjoint-halves split (lowVol 0.0950 in half A, beta 0.1899). Splitting one universe in two is a sharper instrument here than multiplicity correction, because it attacks a different failure -- concentration in a few names rather than the look-elsewhere effect.

crossAssetPortfolio.question: The directive was to apply the strategy to every asset class and decide what works best for each. That has two readings and only one of them works.

mergingUniversesFAILS.what: Pour all 157 symbols -- 29 crypto and 128 equities -- into one ranking and hold the top decile.
mergingUniversesFAILS.result: $1340, 7.1% CAGR, 34.1% drawdown -- worse than either class ranked on its own.
mergingUniversesFAILS.why: Momentum ranks on raw return, and crypto's return distribution is roughly 4x as wide. Crypto took 30% of the long slots while being 18% of the universe, so the book became a levered crypto bet wearing a diversification label. Ranking only compares like with like when the things compared have comparable dispersion.
mergingUniversesFAILS.fixNotAttempted: Volatility-standardising the score before merging would plausibly repair this. It was not tested, and it introduces a free parameter.

fixNowTested.what: The record said volatility-standardising the score before merging would plausibly repair the merge and that it had not been tested. It has now. One change only: rank by formation return divided by realised volatility over the same window. Everything else -- 252/21/21, the book, the costs, the null -- is unchanged, so the comparison isolates the standardisation.
fixNowTested.reading: The diagnosis was right and the untested fix works. Crypto's share of the long slots falls from 30.4% to 11.0% against a neutral 17.9%, the drawdown falls from 33.57% to 14.57%, and the CAGR doubles. Standardising by volatility does not merely reduce crypto's weight, it OVERSHOOTS past neutral -- risk-adjusted momentum prefers the steadier names, which is the low-volatility effect leaking into the ranking.
fixNowTested.butItStillLoses: Merged-and-standardised returns 22.9% at a 14.57% drawdown. Ranking within class and blending the books returns 29.4% at 12.36%. So the answer to 'one universe or two' is still two: standardisation repairs the merge from broken to respectable, and does not reach what keeping the rankings separate achieves.

rankingWithinClassWORKS.construction: Rank inside each class separately at the canonical 252/21/21, run each long-short spread, then combine the two BOOKS. The faster book (crypto, 17.39 rebalances a year) is compounded into the slower book's clock (equities, 11.92) so every period is used exactly once.
rankingWithinClassWORKS.correlationReading: Genuinely negative, not merely uncorrelated. That is what makes the drawdown reduction below real rather than arithmetic. It is also 31 observations, where the standard error on a correlation is about 0.18 -- so -0.235 is barely one standard error from zero and should be read as 'no positive dependence', not as reliable hedging.
rankingWithinClassWORKS.theHeadline: Unchanged in shape by the cost fix, smaller in size. The causal inverse-vol blend returns 29.4% CAGR at a 12.36% drawdown, Sharpe 1.99, against 39.9% at 22.73% (Sharpe 1.50) for crypto alone and 25.0% at 13.55% (Sharpe 1.19) for equities alone. It beats BOTH legs on Sharpe and has a lower drawdown than EITHER, and its weight comes from volatility realised strictly before each period with nothing fitted. The sweep peak is not the result.
rankingWithinClassWORKS.drawdownIsWhereTheDiversificationShows: Every blend from 25/75 to 50/50 lands between 10.34% and 12.88% -- below the equities leg's 13.55% and roughly half the crypto leg's 22.73%. Returns interpolate between the legs; risk does not. That asymmetry is the diversification, and it is the only part of this result large relative to its error bars.

crossAssetPortfolio.arithmeticCorrectionMade: A fourth, smaller one, found before the three above: the first pass combined the books as a weighted sum of LOG returns, which is no portfolio's return. A book rebalanced to fixed weights earns log(w*e^a + (1-w)*e^b), and by Jensen the weighted sum of logs is strictly smaller. Both forcing constraints are asserted in portfolio.test.mjs: at w=1 it must reproduce book A exactly, and +10%/-10% at 50/50 must be exactly flat.
whatThisIsNot: 31 observations. Standard error on a Sharpe is about 0.34 and on a correlation about 0.18, so 2.27 against 1.79 and -0.235 against 0 are both around one standard error. The drawdown halving is the part that is large relative to its error.
One regime. No momentum crash in either class over 2023-2026, so -0.235 has never been measured in the state where both books would be expected to break together.
Two asset classes, not 'every asset class'. Rates, commodities, FX and credit are untested for want of data. Carry needs crypto funding rates this container cannot fetch.
Reproducible from the first commit of this section. Three of its numbers were wrong; only the direction of the finding survived.
crossAssetPortfolio.code: portfolio.mjs (alignReturns aggregating, correlation, bookStats, blend, blendDrawdownPct) with portfolio.test.mjs, 9 tests; xsmom.mjs perYear with 3 tests; portfolio-run.mjs reproduces the table.
crossAssetPortfolio.CORRECTED: 2026-09-04, twice. Four errors in total: the three in threeErrors, plus the short-leg cost credit in shortLegCostCredit, which was not specific to this study but corrupted every long-short level in the campaign. The finding has survived all four. None of its original numbers did.

1_calendar.what: spread(), randomSpreadNull(), testSignal() and walkForward() all divided an annual borrow rate by 12 and annualised CAGR on n/12, and walked per-bar borrow on 252 bars a year.
1_calendar.wrong: True for US equities at a 21-bar rebalance. False for crypto, whose daily bundle carries 365 bars a year, so a 21-bar rebalance comes round 17.39 times a year, not 12.
1_calendar.effect: Every crypto CAGR was computed over 4.17 years of a 2.87-year sample and was therefore UNDERSTATED, and borrow was charged about 40% too often. The crypto spread reads $3130 at 48.7% CAGR, not the $2387 at 40.1% first recorded.
1_calendar.fix: perYear(timestamps) in xsmom.mjs derives periods-per-year and bars-per-year from the timestamps. No universe constant anywhere. Three tests, including one that pins the crypto and equity cases apart.

2_alignment.what: alignReturns paired each equity month with the single most recent crypto period.
2_alignment.wrong: Crypto rebalances 17.4 times a year against equities' 12, so taking one crypto period per equity month silently discarded roughly two of every five. The row labelled 'the crypto book' was a subsample of it.
2_alignment.effect: THE CORRELATION WAS THE ARTIFACT. -0.005 -- the number the whole finding was built on -- becomes -0.235 once every crypto period is used. The conclusion holds and is better supported, but the headline figure was measurement noise from a subsample.
2_alignment.fix: alignReturns now AGGREGATES: a faster book's periods are compounded into the slower book's clock, log returns adding over exactly the right window. It reports how many of the fast book's periods it consumed (45 of 50; 5 fall outside the equity span) so a future subsample cannot hide.

3_drawdown.what: The portfolio table took drawdown from bookStats, which marks only at period ends.
3_drawdown.wrong: A period-end mark never sees an intra-period low. This is the THIRD time the same mistake has produced a number in this project -- it understated a spread's drawdown by 44% once already, and that fix did not generalise to the new code path.
3_drawdown.effect: The crypto spread's real per-bar drawdown is 22.73%, not the 6.17% recorded. Off by a factor of 3.7. Every blend row was similarly flattering.
3_drawdown.fix: blendDrawdownPct walks the union calendar per bar and re-anchors to the costed balance at EACH LEG'S OWN rebalances -- not just the blend's, or crypto's turnover goes uncharged inside most windows. Validated by agreement: at weight 0 it reproduces spread()'s independently-computed 13.53% for equities exactly.

crossAssetPortfolio.lessonForTheRecord: All three errors shared a shape: a constant that was correct for the universe it was written against (12 periods, 252 bars, one period per month, a period-end mark) and silently wrong for the second universe it was then applied to. Crossing asset classes is exactly the operation that breaks such constants, and the code carried four of them into the crossing. Anything derived per-universe should be derived FROM the universe.

tradeLedger.why: Every result in this campaign has been reported per REBALANCE PERIOD -- '19 of 31 periods up'. The stated acceptance criterion is per TRADE: about ten trades a month at a win rate of 40% or better, with the wins covering the losses. Those are different questions and a book can pass one while failing the other. Nothing had measured the second until now.
tradeLedger.construction: A position opens when a symbol enters the held set and closes when it leaves, priced at the rebalance close on both ends. Every trade is charged slippage twice, in and out. Holds still open at the end of the series are reported separately, never marked as if closed -- 3 a side in crypto, 12 a side in equities.
tradeLedger.verdictAgainstTheCriterion: Two of three conditions pass and one fails. WIN RATE passes on every leg -- 42.4% is the worst of the six and the criterion is 40%. 'Wins should win, and offset any losses' passes decisively: the payoff ratio is 1.64 to 2.78, so an average win covers between one and three average losses, and expectancy is positive on every leg net of costs. TRADE COUNT fails: 2.0 a month in crypto and 5.8 in equities, 7.8 for both books together, against a target of about 10.
tradeLedger.theShortLegEarnsItsPlace: 42.4% and 44.3% win rates look weak beside the long legs' 54-55%, but the short legs carry payoff ratios of 2.69 and 1.64 and positive expectancy net of costs (8.8% and 2.9% a trade). A leg that wins less than half the time and still compounds is exactly what the criterion was written to allow.
howTradeCountCouldRISE: More frequent rebalancing. The rebalance interval sets the trade count almost mechanically, and 21 bars is the canonical Jegadeesh-Titman choice rather than an optimised one. A frequency ladder is the obvious next test, and it is a COST question: crypto pays 1.6% round trip, so doubling frequency doubles a charge that already eats a tenth of the average win.
Larger topK. More slots means more names turning over, at the price of diluting the ranking toward the universe mean.

More asset classes. The two books already sum to 7.8 a month, so a third and fourth class reach the target without touching either rule -- and that is the only route on this list that does not trade edge for volume.
tradeLedger.code: trades.mjs (ledger, summarise) with trades.test.mjs, 7 tests; trades-run.mjs reproduces the table. runRotation's rebalance log now records closes for names being dropped as well as held, or every exit would be unpriced.

shortLegCostCredit.found: 2026-09-04, by running two implementations of the same book against each other -- xsmom's spread() against multifactor's runBook(). They disagreed by 21% on crypto and 2% on equities. The ratio of those two numbers is the ratio of their slippage assumptions, which is what named the culprit.
shortLegCostCredit.theBug: Each leg's period return already carries its own turnover cost. The spread takes 0.5*top - 0.5*bot, so the SHORT leg's cost enters with a minus sign and arrives as a CREDIT: the short book was being paid to trade. Both legs turn over at almost exactly the same rate here (0.248 against 0.235 on crypto), so the two costs very nearly cancelled.
shortLegCostCredit.howBigItWas: On crypto at 0.8% slippage, spread() charged 0.5% over fifty rebalances where the honest figure is roughly 20%. Turning slippage from 0 to 0.008 moved the final balance by $18 on $3381 -- a book paying real Kraken taker fees was showing essentially zero cost, and nothing in the numbers looked wrong.
shortLegCostCredit.whereItWas: xsmom.mjs spread() and randomSpreadNull(), factors.mjs testSignal(), xsmom-wf.mjs fit() and walkForward(). Every long-short dollar figure this campaign has produced was inflated by it.
shortLegCostCredit.theFix: runRotation now returns periodCosts alongside periodReturns -- the cost separated from the return -- and every spread adds the short leg's cost back twice: once to undo the credit, once to charge it. Pinned by a test using two symbols that swap rank every period so both legs turn over fully; it asserts the drag exceeds 2% a period and FAILS on the un-fixed code (mutation-checked).
shortLegCostCredit.effectOnSIGNIFICANCE: Small, and in the safe direction. The null carries the same bug, and a random split turns over close to 100% against a ranked book's 25%, so the null received the LARGER spurious credit. Every p-value reported before this fix was therefore conservative, not flattering.
shortLegCostCredit.effectOnLEVELS: Large. The crypto spread falls from $3130 at 48.7% CAGR to $2623 at 39.9%, and its Sharpe from 1.79 to 1.50.
shortLegCostCredit.crossCheckNowAgrees: After the fix the two implementations differ by 5.96% on crypto and 1.32% on equities, and at zero slippage the crypto gap is 5.97% -- so the entire residual is the different warmup (252 bars against 273), which changes the rebalance dates and the holdings. The cost handling matches. Per-bar drawdowns agree to 22.63% and 22.63%, 13.34% and 13.34%.

rebalanceFrequency.question: 'Maximize the number of trades taken, while still being confident in their ability to win.' Rebalance frequency is the dial that sets trade count, and it is a cost question: crypto pays 1.6% round trip.
rebalanceFrequency.discipline: The whole ladder is reported, never the best cell. 21 bars stays the pre-registered canonical choice whatever this shows.
rebalanceFrequency.cryptoReading: Flat. Every rung returns 31-42% at p<=0.002 with a drawdown between 21.9% and 23.7%, across a twelvefold range of turnover, while paying 0.8% slippage a side. That is the opposite of the usual finding, where cost eats a fast rebalance -- and flatness across a parameter is stronger evidence the effect is real than any single rung's number. The practical consequence: crypto trade count can be raised roughly fourfold, from 2 a month to about 8, without visible damage to the edge. The variation from $2194 to $2737 across rungs is the noise floor, not a signal about which rung is best.
rebalanceFrequency.code: frequency-run.mjs, which takes its trade counts from the real ledger rather than a bars-per-year formula -- that assumption has already been wrong once here.
